summary: Atlas cannot distinguish shared-milieu edges from independent convergence
description:
An accepted PARALLELS edge asserts that two chunks make the same conceptual
claim. It does not record WHY they do, and the Atlas presents every edge
identically. Three quite different situations render the same:

  (a) genuine independent convergence  (Plato Timaeus <-> yoga-sutras IV.12)
  (b) shared milieu / common source    (Johnston and Hartmann are both
                                        Theosophists reading through one lens)
  (c) one text quoting the other's tradition  (declined here, but only because
                                        a reviewer noticed - see 43a62e3f)

## Evidence from the yoga-sutras pass

Seven accepted edges were flagged genealogical during review. Two are
structural rather than incidental:

1. yoga-sutras IV.12 ARGUES ITS OWN CROSS-TRADITION CASE. Johnston's
   commentary quotes John 8:58, Revelation, a Mahatma letter and Bjorklund
   inside the chunk body. Five edges now radiate from it to Plato, Plotinus
   (x2) and Ouspensky (x2). Every one is accurate as a text-to-text match.
   Together they will read in the Atlas as five traditions independently
   arriving at the eternal-Now doctrine. That is not what happened - the
   comparison is the chunk's content.

2. THE BOEHME IN THIS CORPUS IS A THEOSOPHICAL EDITION. Hartmann's note 251:2
   glosses Boehme as "when the disciple becomes an accepted *Chela*, his evil
   *Karma* begins to assert itself". Roughly ten accepted Boehme edges come
   through that lens, and Johnston reads Patanjali through the same one.

## What is wanted

Not withholding these edges - they are true. Something that lets the Atlas (or
a reader) distinguish "these two traditions independently reached this" from
"these two authors shared a bookshelf".

Possible shapes:
- a nullable `relation_basis` on edges: convergent | shared_milieu | quotation
- or a per-source `milieu` / `edition_lens` field in sources/manifest.toml
  (Johnston 1912, Hartmann 1891, Mead, Ouspensky/Bragdon 1920 are one network),
  letting the Atlas compute it rather than asking reviewers to tag each edge
- the manifest approach is cheaper and less error-prone; reviewers should not
  be re-deriving publication history per edge

Downstream: this is a presentation/provenance concern, not a reason to change
node 14's bar.
